entry: Capital and largest city of the Free State province in [[South Africa]] (pop., 2011: 256,185). Traditionally called the country's "judicial capital," it hosts the Supreme Court of Appeal, while the Constitutional Court has been in [[Johannesburg]] since 1994. The city was founded in 1846 as a British fort by Major Henry Douglas Warden. Popularly known as the "City of Roses," it has numerous museums. Its Sesotho name, Mangaung, means "place of [[Cheetah|cheetahs]]."

[[Website]] whose basic unit is a "post" or "entry," usually presented in reverse chronological order. The term is a truncation of "weblog." In the 2000s most blogs were run by one individual, often on a single topic; from the 2010s, multi-author blogs run by newspapers, universities, and other institutions became common. Late-1990s publishing tools let non-technical users post without much experience with [[HTML]] or programming. By the 2010s most blogs were interactive, allowing reader comments. A 2022 estimate counted over 600 million public blogs.

American rock band and early pioneer of new wave. Formed in New York City in 1974 by Debbie Harry and Chris Stein, the group emerged from the CBGB punk scene. Its album *Parallel Lines* (1978) brought international success, with hits including "Heart of Glass," "Call Me," and "Rapture," the first *Billboard* number-one single to feature rap vocals. The band disbanded in 1982 and re-formed in 1997. Inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2006, it has sold over 40 million records worldwide.

1985 epic historical novel by [[Cormac McCarthy]]. Set on the [[American frontier]], it follows a teenager from [[Tennessee]], known only as "the Kid," who joins the Glanton gang of scalp hunters. The gang massacred American Indians and others in the U.S.–Mexico borderlands from 1849 to 1850. Judge Holden, a physically massive, highly educated gang member, emerges as the antagonist. Its initial reception was lukewarm, but it is now widely regarded as McCarthy's masterpiece, and some have labeled it the Great American Novel.

Light amber-colored liquid component of [[Blood|blood]] in which blood cells are absent. It makes up about 55% of total blood volume and is up to 95% water by volume. Dissolved [[Protein|proteins]] make up 6–8% of plasma, along with [[Glucose|glucose]], clotting factors, electrolytes, hormones, [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]], and [[Oxygen|oxygen]]. Plasma can be separated from whole blood by adding an anticoagulant and spinning the sample in a [[Centrifuge|centrifuge]]. Fresh frozen plasma is on the World Health Organization's Model List of Essential Medicines and is critical in treating trauma with blood loss.

Pressure exerted by circulating blood on the walls of blood vessels. Most of this pressure results from the heart pumping blood through the [[Circulatory system|circulatory system]]. Unqualified, the term refers to pressure in a brachial artery, where it is most commonly measured. It is expressed as systolic pressure over diastolic pressure in millimeters of mercury (mmHg). A normal adult resting reading is under 120/80 mmHg, according to the American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology. Globally, the average has changed little since 1975, at approximately 127/79 mmHg in men and 122/77 mmHg in women. Baroreceptors regulate pressure in the short term by acting through the [[Nervous system|nervous system]] and [[Endocrine system|endocrine system]]. Consistently high pressure, called [[Hypertension|hypertension]], raises the risk of [[Stroke|stroke]], heart disease, and [[Kidney|kidney]] failure.

Concentration of [[Glucose|glucose]] in the blood, also called glycemia. The body tightly regulates blood glucose as part of metabolic homeostasis. For a 70 kg (154 lb) human, approximately four grams of dissolved glucose is maintained in the [[Blood plasma|blood plasma]] at all times. Glucose not circulating is stored as [[Glycogen|glycogen]] in the [[Liver|liver]] and skeletal muscle. [[Insulin|Insulin]], a hormone produced in the [[Pancreas|pancreas]], primarily regulates the uptake of glucose into cells. The human brain consumes approximately 60% of blood glucose in fasting, sedentary individuals. Abnormally high levels, called hyperglycemia, characterize [[Diabetes|diabetes mellitus]], while low levels are called [[Hypoglycemia|hypoglycemia]].

Laboratory analysis performed on a blood sample, usually drawn from a [[Vein|vein]] in the arm with a hypodermic needle or by fingerprick. Tests for individual components, such as [[Glucose|glucose]] or cholesterol, are often grouped into a blood panel or blood work. Blood tests help determine physiological and biochemical states, including [[Disease|disease]], mineral content, drug effectiveness, and organ function, and are often used in [[Health care|health care]]. Typical clinical panels include a basic metabolic panel or a complete blood count. Common types also include lipid profiles and thyroid function tests. Blood tests are used in drug tests to detect drug abuse.

Intravenous transfer of blood products into a human or other animal. Apart from major trauma, whole blood is rarely transfused in modern practice; instead, components such as [[Red blood cell|red blood cells]], plasma, platelets, and clotting factors are given. [[White blood cell|White blood cells]] are not commonly transfused. Compatibility testing based on the ABO and Rh blood group systems prevents acute hemolytic reactions. Anticoagulants such as citrate enabled safe storage and large-scale use during [[World War I]]. Risks include allergic responses and immune-mediated hemolysis.

Classification of blood based on [[Antibody|antibodies]] and antigens on the surface of [[Red blood cell|red blood cells]]. The ABO and Rh systems are the two most important for [[Blood transfusion|transfusion]] compatibility, producing types A, B, AB, and O, with + or − denoting RhD status. Type A plasma contains anti-B antibodies, type B plasma contains anti-A antibodies, and type O plasma contains both. Type O− is the universal donor for red cells, and AB+ is the universal recipient. Rh antibodies develop after exposure through transfusion or [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]], and Rh incompatibility can cause hemolytic disease of the newborn. The International Society of Blood Transfusion recognized 49 human blood group systems as of September 2026.

Large [[Hound|scent hound]] dog breed used for tracking. It was originally bred for hunting [[Deer|deer]], [[Wild boar|wild boar]], and rabbits, and has been used to track people since the [[Middle Ages]]. The breed is believed to descend from hounds kept at the Abbey of Saint-Hubert in [[Belgium]]. Its keen [[Sense of smell|sense of smell]] lets it discern human scent over large distances and long periods. Police and law enforcement agencies around the world use bloodhounds to track fugitives, missing people, and lost pets.

Deliberate withdrawal of blood from a patient, by a physician or by [[Leech|leeches]], to prevent or cure illness. Based on the ancient belief that bodily "humors" must stay in balance, it was common medical practice from antiquity until the late 19th century. Studies in the early 19th century began to show its harm, and modern medicine has abandoned it except for therapeutic phlebotomy in conditions such as hemochromatosis. The traditional practice is regarded as [[Pseudoscience|pseudoscience]], though it persists in some [[Alternative medicine|alternative medicine]].

Predominantly African American [[Gang|street gang]] founded in Los Angeles, California. Known for its rivalry with the [[Crips]], it is identified by the color red and by hand signs. Its subgroups, called "sets," differ in colors, clothing, operations, and political ideas. The gang spread throughout the United States after its founding, and by the 1990s had proliferated to over 100 cities.

Digital [[Optical disc|optical disc]] format designed to supersede the [[DVD]], storing several hours of high-definition video. Released worldwide on June 20, 2006, it takes its name from the blue laser used to read it, which allows greater storage density than the red laser of DVDs. Conventional discs hold 25 GB per layer, and dual-layer discs (50 GB) are the industry standard for feature-length video. [[Sony]] unveiled the first prototypes in October 2000. Toshiba discontinued the competing HD DVD format in February 2008.

Color between violet and cyan on the visible spectrum of light. It is one of the three [[Primary color|primary colors]] in the [[RGB color model|RGB]] additive color model. Blue generally describes colors perceived from light with a dominant wavelength of approximately 450 and 495 nanometers. Clear daytime skies and deep seas appear blue because of [[Rayleigh scattering]]. [[Lapis lazuli]] was used in ancient Egypt for ornament, and in the Renaissance it was ground into [[Ultramarine|ultramarine]], the most expensive of all pigments. In the United States and Europe, blue is the color that both men and women most often choose as their favorite. Because blue has been associated with harmony, it was chosen for the flags of the [[United Nations]] and the [[European Union]].

Major tributary of the [[Nile]], flowing through Ethiopia and Sudan. It originates at Lake Tana in Ethiopia and travels about 1,450 km (900 mi). Along with the [[White Nile|White Nile]], it is one of the Nile's two major tributaries, supplying about 85.6% of the Nile's water during the rainy season. Known in Ethiopia as the Abay, the river joins the White Nile at [[Khartoum]]. Its flow, driven by monsoon rains in the [[Ethiopian Highlands|Ethiopian highlands]], peaks from July to September and supports [[Hydropower|hydropower]] development. Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam has sparked international tensions over water security involving [[Egypt]] and Sudan.

Physiographic province of the larger [[Appalachian Mountains]] system in the eastern United States. It extends about 550 miles (885 km) southwest from southern [[Pennsylvania]] to [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]]. Isoprene released by trees into the atmosphere contributes to a bluish haze that gives the range its name. Shenandoah and [[Great Smoky Mountains National Park|Great Smoky Mountains]] national parks lie within the province and are linked by the 469-mile Blue Ridge Parkway. Mount Mitchell in North Carolina, at 6,684 feet, is the highest peak east of the Mississippi River.

1986 American neo-noir mystery film written and directed by [[David Lynch]]. A college student played by Kyle MacLachlan finds a severed human ear in a field and uncovers a criminal conspiracy involving a nightclub singer played by Isabella Rossellini. Its initial critical reception was divided. The film earned Lynch his second Academy Award nomination for Best Director and is now widely regarded as one of his masterpieces.

Four highly venomous species of [[Octopus|octopus]] in the genus *Hapalochlaena*. They live in tide pools and [[Coral reef|coral reefs]] of the Pacific and Indian Oceans, from [[Japan]] to [[Australia]], and eat small [[Crustacean|crustaceans]] such as crabs and shrimp. Their yellowish skin shows blue and black rings that change dramatically when they are threatened. Measuring 12 to 20 cm (5 to 8 in), they are among the world's most venomous marine animals; their venom contains the neurotoxin tetrodotoxin.

Species of baleen whale and the largest animal known to have ever existed. Reaching 29.9–30.5 m (98–100 ft) and weighing up to 190–200 t, it has a slender, grayish-blue body. Blue whales are filter feeders that eat almost exclusively [[Krill|krill]], and populations migrate between summer feeding areas near the poles and winter breeding grounds near the tropics. [[Whaling|Whalers]] hunted the species nearly to extinction until the International Whaling Commission banned blue whale hunting in 1966. The International Union for Conservation of Nature has listed it as endangered as of 2018.

Perennial flowering plant with blue or purple berries, in the genus *Vaccinium*. Commercial blueberries are native to [[North America]], where lowbush (wild) varieties have small, pea-size berries and highbush (cultivated) varieties have larger berries on taller bushes. Highbush varieties were introduced into Europe during the 1930s. Their color comes from [[Anthocyanin|anthocyanins]], pigments concentrated in the skin. Plants range from 10 cm (4 in) to 4 m (13 ft) tall. In 2025, [[Canada]] was the leading producer of lowbush blueberries, while China produced 35% of the world's highbush supply.

Music genre and musical form that originated among [[African Americans]] in the [[Deep South]] of the United States around the 1860s. It incorporated spirituals, work songs, and field hollers. Its most common structure is the twelve-bar [[Chord (music)|chord]] progression, and "blue notes," usually flattened thirds, fifths, or sevenths, are essential to its sound. The form is ubiquitous in [[Jazz|jazz]], [[Rhythm and blues|rhythm and blues]], and [[Rock and roll|rock and roll]]. Electric blues developed after [[World War II]], opening the genre to a wider audience, especially white listeners.

Short-range wireless technology standard for exchanging data between fixed and mobile devices. In its most common mode, transmission power is limited to 2.5 milliwatts, giving a range of up to 10 meters (33 ft). It uses UHF radio waves in the ISM bands, from 2.402 GHz to 2.48 GHz. It is used to connect phones and music players to wireless headphones, speakers, and car audio. The Bluetooth Special Interest Group, with more than 35,000 member companies, oversees the specification and manages qualification. As of 2021, 4.7 billion Bluetooth [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuit]] chips shipped annually.

Australian animated preschool television series created by Joe Brumm. It was commissioned by the [[Australian Broadcasting Corporation]] and the [[BBC]] and premiered on ABC Kids on October 1, 2018. It follows Bluey, a Blue Heeler puppy, her sister Bingo, and their family through [[Play (activity)|imaginative play]]. The show has won three Logie Awards, three AACTA Awards, an International Emmy Kids Award in 2019, and a Peabody Award in 2024. A feature film, *The Bluey Movie*, is scheduled for release on August 6, 2027.

Physical injury caused by forceful impact without penetration of the body's surface. Blunt trauma contrasts with penetrating trauma, in which an object pierces the skin and creates an open wound. It commonly results from [[Traffic collision|road traffic collisions]], [[Assault|assaults]], sports injuries, and falls, which are common among the elderly. Injuries range from [[Bruise|bruises]] and [[Concussion|concussions]] to internal bleeding and [[Bone fracture|bone fractures]]. Severity depends on the force of impact, the body area affected, and underlying medical conditions. Blunt trauma to the head and severe blood loss are the most likely causes of death from blunt force injury.
